Every prime number greater than 2 is odd.why: Rarely in exactly this form, but stored as its equivalent '2 is the only even prime', which is stated thousands of times; Wikipedia states the rule directly. It also follows from the definition of a prime (an even number above 2 has 2 as a divisor), so a model has both a stored and a derived route; the frequency of the equivalent form makes stored the better estimate (unlikely to be derived).

sources.quote: Therefore, every prime number other than 2 is an odd number, and is called an odd prime.

notes: Delete of replace-0007's rule. The primes named in the prompt go only through the rule: determinate 'does not know'. Unlike the replace, the delete leaves consistent worlds: forgetting a rule contradicts nothing, so a model may keep a well-known member's value stored by name (or worked out without the rule) while the rule itself is gone, as in any TBox delete (README, Delete under determinacy). 7's parity and the parity of 3 × 5 = 15 are each known by name (or by a one-line computation) or reached through the rule; the choices are independent, so there are 4 worlds. The by-name worlds are likely here, since small numbers' parities are known directly. Verifier: the new member is now an unnamed prime with millions of digits, since the Mersenne form 2^n − 1 showed it odd without the rule.
